content: Geriatrics is a specialized branch of medicine that concentrates on promoting health, preventing disease, and managing disabilities in older adults. It is distinct from gerontology, which is the study of the aging process itself. The term geriatrics originates from the Greek words geron, meaning old man, and iatros, meaning healer. This term was introduced in 1909 by Dr. Ignatz Leo Nascher. Interestingly, it shares linguistic roots with the Sanskrit word jara, which also means old. In the United States, geriatricians are primary care physicians who are board-certified in either family medicine or internal medicine. They undergo additional training to earn the Certificate of Added Qualifications (CAQ) in geriatric medicine. In the United Kingdom, most geriatricians work as hospital-based physicians, although some focus on community geriatrics. Initially a distinct specialty, geriatrics has been integrated into general medicine since the late 1970s, and most geriatricians are accredited in both fields. Specialized geriatric services include orthogeriatrics, which involves collaboration with orthopedic surgery and focuses on osteoporosis and rehabilitation; psychogeriatrics, which addresses dementia, depression, and other mental health conditions common in older adults; and rehabilitation services. Rehabilitation may also encompass intermediate care, where patients are referred by hospitals or family doctors for short-term, intensive physical therapy aimed at restoring musculoskeletal function. This is particularly relevant for recovery from joint, tendon, or ligament repairs, as well as for addressing health deterioration caused by medication mismanagement, which can impair an elderly person's ability to live independently. Modern geriatrics in the UK owes much to Dr. Marjorie Warren, often referred to as the Mother of Geriatrics. Dr. Warren emphasized the importance of rehabilitation in the care of older adults. Drawing from her experiences as a physician in a London workhouse infirmary, she developed the concept that merely providing sustenance to older individuals until their death was insufficient. Instead, she advocated for proper diagnosis, treatment, care, and support. Her work demonstrated that even bedridden patients could regain some level of independence with appropriate assessment and treatment. The practice of geriatrics in the UK has a rich history of multidisciplinary collaboration, valuing contributions from various professions beyond medicine to optimize the well-being and independence of older adults. Another key figure in British geriatrics is Bernard Isaacs, who identified the giants of geriatrics: incontinence, immobility, impaired intellect, and instability. Isaacs argued that most common problems in older adults could be traced back to one of these giants. The care of older adults in the UK has been further advanced by the implementation of the National Service Frameworks for Older People, which highlights critical areas for attention. One of the most pressing challenges in geriatrics today is the prevention and treatment of delirium. Delirium is a condition in which hospitalized elderly patients become confused and disoriented due to the unfamiliar and often stressful hospital environment. This condition can lead to a decline in the patient’s overall health, prolong hospital stays, and result in additional health complications. Treating delirium involves keeping patients mentally stimulated and oriented to reality, as well as providing specialized care to meet their needs. The Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP), developed at Yale New Haven Hospital, has been implemented in several hospitals to prevent delirium and improve the quality of care for elderly patients. Yale New Haven Hospital has since expanded HELP into the more comprehensive Elder Horizons Program, which aims not only to prevent delirium but also to maintain mobility, functional independence, and cognitive health. Pharmacological management in older adults is a critical area of focus due to the physiological and psychological changes associated with aging. These changes can alter drug absorption, effectiveness, and side effect profiles. For example, changes in the gastrointestinal system, body fat and muscle distribution, and drug elimination processes can all impact how medications work in older individuals. Another significant concern is the improper administration or use of potentially inappropriate medications, which can lead to dangerous drug interactions. Additionally, elderly patients, particularly those with memory loss or cognitive impairments, may struggle to adhere to their prescribed medication regimens. Studies have shown that 25% of older adults admit to skipping doses or cutting them in half, and one-third report noncompliance with their medication schedules. This highlights the importance of monitoring and supporting medication adherence in this population.
